title: No, We Can't Do Whatever We Darn Well Please in the Classroom
author: Janetos, Harriett
summary: Harriett Janetos challenges the framing — common in pushback against structured literacy reform — that teachers should be sole determiners of their own instructional practice, arguing that professional autonomy without professional accountability produces outcomes that systematically harm struggling readers. She distinguishes between legitimate professional expertise, which justifies practitioner autonomy, and the structural conditions that routinely prevent teachers from developing genuine expertise in reading instruction: inadequate pre-service training, flawed professional development, and instructional materials that contradict the science of reading. Janetos argues that the appeal to teacher autonomy has been weaponised to resist evidence-based practice, conflating the right to make informed professional decisions with the right to make uninformed ones. Drawing on Daniel Willingham and others, she shows how institutional rather than intentional decisions drive poor reading instruction. The article concludes that teachers deserve better training and better materials — and that receiving them comes with professional obligations that genuine expertise entails.
points: I simply cannot find any dictionary that defines a professional as someone who can do whatever he or she pleases.
The appeal to teacher autonomy has been weaponised to resist evidence-based practice — conflating the right to make informed professional decisions with the right to make uninformed ones.
How can teachers already NOT know? It's a crime that teachers don't know all this stuff — principles of learning are the first things you'd learn in introduction to cognitive psychology.

Preservice programs that do not impart current research, nonexistent or flawed PD that reinforces ideology rather than effectiveness — these are institutional failures, not evidence of teacher expertise.
Teachers who choose methods based on what everyone else in the building is doing are making institutional decisions, not professional ones — and students who struggle with reading pay the price.
quotes: Problems arise when a teacher who has complete freedom to select instructional practices lacks the knowledge to distinguish between: tradition and targeted teaching ideology and pedagogy belief and evidence Agency isn’t the freedom to indiscriminately bypass every single science of reading recommendation—it is the freedom to exercise skilled analysis to determine which recommendations pose real obstacles and which ones represent evidence-based practices to counter habits, myths, or fads.

She Says: I remember following up with one parent and gently reminding them that they hadn’t sent back the levelled book that their child had been practicing at home, and the mom emailed me back and said: ‘Oh, yeah, I’m waiting until she can do it with the pictures covered, and then we’ll really know she can read it.’ And I remember thinking: Well that’s kinda mean—she’s not going to be able to read it with the pictures covered.

Preservice programs that do not impart current research; nonexistent or flawed PD that reinforces ideology rather than instructional effectiveness; overstuffed timetables that impinge on a teacher’s ability to problem solve; and ineffective materials like predictable text that mislead students about how to develop word recognition.

I’m not saying that a reflexive resistance to the SOR movement is the result of a herd mentality—which can be used to argue against both sides of the reading divide—but I am making this analogy to teachers: A teacher who wants to make an informed choice must ask: Is this instructional practice actually supported by evidence?

Looking at the materials available to me before teaching kindergarten, it didn’t take me long to realize that predictable text is based on introducing high-frequency words (HFW) through a repeated sentence structure on each page—same sentence frame but with a different non-decodable word completing the sentence.

Autonomy The refrain I hear from those who are legitimately concerned about legislative overreach related to reading instruction—like banning the three-cueing system instead of contextualizing it—is that teachers should be the sole determiners of decisions about which practices to use in their classrooms.

Teachers who choose to use these methods and materials can certainly make an informed decision about what these choices might offer their students, but more often than not, these decisions are institutional rather than intentional, adopted because that’s what everyone else in the building is doing.
